 Weekend Plans With ‘Frasier’ Star Kelsey Grammer
 Frasier Crane is so iconic that Kelsey quotes him, too.
 Lauren Bair • Nov 21, 2026 Listen Listen • 12 min 1 x Your browser does not support the audio element. Weekend Plans is our exclusive lifestyle feature where we highlight the real off-duty routines of the most exciting people in culture.  
 This weekend, Kelsey Grammer — the acclaimed actor behind psychiatrist Dr. Frasier Crane on “Frasier” and “Cheers” — chats with The Daily Wire about his new coffee table book “ The America Opus ,” t he ’70s th riller that nearly scarred him for life, the seminal works he draws on daily, and how this former surfer teen turned unlikely odds into a shining example of the American dream.  
 *** 
 If you were wondering how similar Kelsey Grammer is to the character he made famous, we were already discussing world-renowned opera singer Plácido Domingo just minutes into our chat. I grew up watching “Frasier,” and my parents quote the show all the time.  
 “Even we quote it sometimes,” Kelsey says with a smile. I have no proof, but I think my IQ rose a point just because of this. He recalls a scene from season 11 that he filmed with the late Sir Patrick Stewart . “I was working with [Patrick] last year … and I told him I’ve been writing some stuff, and he said, ‘Oh yeah, I hope you’re not writing about me.’ Well, I actually was,” Kelsey says. “I wrote about how there was a scene when Niles and Frasier met this opera director — who was Patrick Stewart — and he’s on the phone. He says, ‘Plácido,’ and then Niles and Frasier go, ‘Plácido Domingo.’ We do that all the time in my house.” 
 Having starred in several pop-culture behemoths (he also voices Sideshow Bob on “The Simpsons”), Kelsey’s been a recognizable face in entertainment since the ’80s. But he won’t succumb to the whim of every fan just to stay relevant.  
 “ I don’t really do much for my fans, honestly. Except field really strange requests,” he says after I warn him we’ll be going behind the scenes, so to speak. Alluding to oddball demands of fan texts, he adds, “I don’t even know who any of these people are. I just keep blocking them or reporting it as spam. Then somebody else shows up. You think, how is this possible?” 
 We briefly joke that he could be making a lot of money answering these types of requests on another platform that shall remain nameless. But he’s carved out a lauded career without relying on easy cash grabs, all while defying the odds. 
 Kelsey faced tragedy early in his life when his father Frank was murdered. Several years later, his sister Karen suffered a similar fate. Somewhere in between navigating waves of grief as a teen surfer in Florida, Kelsey gained acceptance into the prestigious Juilliard School in New York City to study drama on not much more than a whim. 
 “I was a surfer and I sang in churches,” Kelsey explains. After acting in a play in 11th grade (“The Little Foxes” by Lillian Hellman), he remembers, “It was actually a pretty good play and I was good in it. I thought to myself, well, I could do this the rest of my life.” 
 He enrolled in music camp at Florida State University that summer, and when he was asked by his high school counselor what he wanted to do, Kelsey told him, “I think I wanna give this acting thing a shot. I said, ‘I hear Juilliard is the best school in America, and then I heard Carnegie Mellon’s right up there too, so I’m gonna apply to them.’” 
 Just Juilliard, where the acceptance rate is famously in the single digits. “I was too stupid to be intimidated,” Kelsey laughs. He recalls British actor and producer John Houseman judging his audition from the shadowy corners of the auditorium, along with speech coach Edith Skinner and vocal coach Elizabeth Smith. 
 “John Houseman said from the dark, ‘Do you intend to make acting your profession?’” Kelsey imitates John’s accent with booming gravitas. “I looked at him and I thought, ‘Well, I flew up here from Fort Lauderdale, didn’t I?’ It’s one of my more inspired responses. But they let me in.” 
 Now collaborating on the Rolls-Royce of coffee table books with “The America Opus,” Kelsey reflects on peak Americana with a stunning 50-pound keepsake, or a smaller version better suited to holding in your lap. Considering the foreword from President Donald Trump — and previous comments Kelsey’s made about possibly entering politics later in life — I ask if he’ll be throwing his hat in the ring. 
 “No,” he says. “That’s funny. Well … 2028 would actually probably have to be the time for me, wouldn’t it?” The door remains officially cracked. As for the message of his book, Kelsey muses, “We’ve gotten it right more than we’ve gotten it wrong.” 
 “Countries are full of savage beginnings,” he says, describing America as a reflection of its people. “Its true north has always been the people … a group of individuals that all believe in something special … their future, their creator, their destiny. America is like no other place. It enshrines that right for you to go ahead and figure out what your dream is and do something about it. That’s why I’m here.” 
 Casually aspirational 
 “I’m pretty easygoing, you know, shorts and a T-shirt most of the time at home,” Kelsey confirms when I ask how his off-camera life is different from his public persona. But he and his wife Kayte Walsh may be on the verge of a couple’s makeover. 
 “I’ll show up in public looking semi-decent, but Kayte and I talk about it all the time, like we should dress up more — like Cary Grant,” Kelsey says. “Mostly the white shirt and a nice pair of slacks and a blazer. I do have that as sort of my go-to for public perception.” 
 Still, Kelsey laments a recent foot procedure that had him stuck wearing a surgical boot. “I’ve had a couple of tabloid guys snap a shot while I’m walking in to pick up E. Baldi [Tuscan food], and they’re like, ‘Oh, he looks great.’” I saw the pics. Somehow Kelsey still made post-op look sartorial.  
 Mornings at Kelsey’s house 
 “I tend to wake up early. I usually get up around 5:30,” Kelsey confirms. Taking advantage of a quiet home, he gets right to work. “I’ll do a little writing. I’m working on a memoir, so that’s been going great. But then as soon as the baby wakes up, in he comes and we’re into our morning.” 
 Breakfast might be scrambled eggs depending on the mood, but forget the local coffee shop because the best part of waking up is Kelsey’s perfect cup. “Pretty much every morning I’m the guy that makes the coffees,” he says. “For Kayte, I make an Americano with heavy cream. For myself, I make a breve latte.” 
 Now that he’s mastered his La Marzocco coffee machine, Kelsey says he’s ruined on outside coffee. “I make great coffee,” he says. “It’s gotten to the point where, when I go away, I usually don’t even try to get a cup of coffee.”  
 As for maintaining his fitness into his 70s, Kelsey’s got a guy for that. “I have a Russian kid named Pasha who comes and works me out pretty much every day,” he says. He was linked up with the trainer through Kayte’s brother Phil, who trains professional footballers. “Pasha is an ex-professional soccer player,” Kelsey explains. The actor also admits he’s had “terribly flat feet since I was 8 years old,” but regular physical therapy and a few bionic adjustments have added a bounce to his step.  
 Food on the table 
 Along with his four adult children from previous relationships, Kelsey shares four younger children with Kayte. But with their ages ranging from toddler to teen, there’s rarely a consensus on what to eat. 
 “Kayte’s a wonderful cook, but she’s a vegetarian,” Kelsey laughs. “So I do the meat. The boys like hot dogs sometimes, or steak.” But having developed a takeout routine since the lockdowns in Los Angeles, Kelsey says welcoming their youngest only extended the ritual that serves as a quick fix for daily meal planning. 
 “So there’s Faith, Gabriel, James, and now the baby,” Kelsey explains. “We’ll say, ‘Maybe pasta tonight?’ And they’d say, ‘Yeah, but we don’t like penne.’ That’s Faith. Then Gabe doesn’t like tomato sauce with it, and then James says, ‘I’ll eat the star kind.’ So it means we’re cooking three different meals every night. I finally said, ‘Look, one of these days it’s just gonna be whatever your mom’s making that’s what you’re eating, and that’s gonna be it.’” 
 In good company 
 Considering he’s got the world at his fingertips, Kelsey’s favorite way to spend time with his family is surprisingly down to earth. “Popcorn and a movie,” he says, sounding legitimately chuffed just thinking about it. “I make the popcorn and then we just put on a movie in the theater.”  
 “James has a sort of encyclopedic knowledge of all animated movies, so we watch a lot of those,” he says. On rare occasions when James lets others weigh in on the feature presentation, the Grammers endure decision fatigue just like every other family. “They say, ‘Nothing out of the nineties … none of those romantic comedies.’” 
 But one classic always makes the cut. “[James’] favorite movie is ‘Ghostbusters,’ and I’m okay with that,” Kelsey says. “What’s even weirder is Gabriel and James’ favorite movie for quite a while was also ‘Jaws.’” Kelsey remembers watching the Spielberg thriller when it came out. 
 “[‘Jaws’] messed me up,” he laughs. “The first time I saw it in the theater in 1975, I actually canceled my diving trip. The next day I called my friend and said, ‘You know, I’m a little busy.’” But Kelsey knew he’d never get over it if he didn’t face his fears. “We went diving two days later, but yeah. That was an effective movie.” 
 The art of living well 
 As you might expect, Kelsey studies society’s masterworks on the regular. “I tend to read from all sorts of things all the time,” he says. As for his current nightstand stack, he says, “I’ve been reading ‘Love Letters,’ the A.R. Gurney play. I’m always reading from ‘Paradise Lost.’ I’m always reading bits of the Bible. There’s a great poet named James Merrill who did a wonderful thing called ‘Scripts for the Pageant,’ which I refer to all the time. It’s one of my favorite pieces.” 
 When Kelsey casually tells me “I was reading a little Plato the other day … I’m a real nerd,” I assure him a nerd of his caliber may be better known as a Renaissance man. While he says he doesn’t listen to as much music as he used to, he’s realized somewhat of a lifelong dream. 
 “ I recently bought a McIntosh amplifier, which was like a wet dream of an adolescent young man,” he says. “I got a turntable and I have amazing speakers, so I’m listening to vinyl … Frank Sinatra, Seals & Crofts, Todd Rundgren, Leon Russell, some of the classics.” I’m delighted with details that seem so deeply Kelsey Grammer-ish. 
 Straight to the heart 
 Looking back at decades in the business, Kelsey says there’s something Hollywood may be missing now. “Hollywood’s always been sort of a mixture of people with a big agenda that they want to insert into their creativity,” he says. “They’re not telling great stories lately. Honestly, they’ve kind of reduced the size of the human heart.” 
 “Faulkner — when he won the Nobel Prize for Literature — gave some advice to the young writer in his acceptance speech. He said, ‘Whatever you’re writing about, make sure it’s about the human heart, because if it isn’t, it’s about nothing.’ We’ve fallen into doing a lot of nothing,” Kelsey explains. “If I see another movie about a hitman, honestly. Why is treating each other horribly cool or edgy? It doesn’t make a lot of sense to me. I’d like to get back to that human heart thing and tell a nice story.” 
 Speaking of great stories, you can take this advice from someone who beat the odds to earn a permanent place in the cultural canon. “Don’t quit,” Kelsey says. “Talent, tenacity, intention … Those are the three things you have to have. If you know where you’re going, you’ll get there.”
